Title: VTES Sideboards (Was RE: Time for a Change)

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Sten wrote:
>>Either that or (starts diving for cover) a sideboard. The merits of a
sideboard (still ducking desperately) would most probably be that we'd
see clan/sect/whatever -hosers used a lot more.>>

Sideboards are useless in VTES.

You only play three games (sometimes only two) before the finals. In each of
those games, you are quite likely to be playing against completely different
opponents.

You can't sideboard before your first game, 'cause you don't know what you are
playing against.

You can only sideboard before your second game if you happen to know what your
opponents are playing, which means either you were in a game with them in the
first round or you have "scouted" information (which might be wrong). This
gives a disadvantage to folks who haven't seen their opponents decks.

Third game and final is the same as the second.

Including sideboards is simply asking for crazy rules about "scouting", which
is just stupid.

Tournament Babylon 5 CCG worked much like VTES in many ways--you would play
against multiple opponents in a small number of games (3 or 4, just like VTES),
but had a sideboard option. The game was structured such a way that you knew
what faction your opponents were playing before the game started, and as such,
you could sideboard based on the knowledge of your opponent's factions, and not
need "scouted" knowledge, in theory. Sadly, this wasn't actually the case, and
scouting your opponents was a huge part of the game (and using your sideboard),
such that they had to invent all sorts of really absurd anti-scouting rules for
tournaments, that didn't actually work, and didn't actually prevent scouting
your opposition. People constantly argued over this very point. It was really
dumb. Consequently, our local group didn't use sideboards in out B5
tournaments, 'cause they were stupid.

Sideboards work in Magic because you generally play best 2 out of 3 vs your
opponent--you sit down to play a match with your unmodified deck, play a game,
and then sideboard for the next game based on your in game knowledge of your
opponent. Same goes for the thrid game. As far as I understand, use of scouted
information is limited a great deal, as you *must* play with your registered,
unmodified (i.e. un-sideboarded) deck in the first game of a match, even
against opponents you have played against before, thus, scouting and out of
match knowledge is not particularly useful, or at least minimized.

VTES doesn't work like this. You play 3 or 4 games, total (as opposed to, like,
18-24 in a Magic tournament), against different opponents every time (as
opposed to playing against the same opponent 2 out of 3 games).

Sideboards in VTES will not work, cannot work, and are just a bad idea.

Messages.Author: Thomas Pichler
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija <pd...@aol.comantispam> wrote:
[snip]
: Sideboards in VTES will not work, cannot work, and are just a bad idea.

Between-game sideboards will not work, but those are not the only kind.

The old Middle Earth: The Wizards CCG used an in-game sideboard, i.e.
cards from your sideboard could enter your deck during play.

Something like this could be useful in VTES - the problem is coming up
with a VTES-workable concept.

Key questions:
1. How many cards should the sideboard contain?
I suspect 15-20 card sideboards should be plenty - at least I can't off
the top of my head of any game I've recently played where that wouldn't
have been large enough.
[Well, unless I wanted to include one of every clan hoser... but, we
wouldn't want sideboards to be large enough to allow that AND useful cards
on top of that.]

2. How are cards exchanged between library and sideboard?
[One might ask whether cards are actually exchanged or just added to the
library from the sideboard - the latter would imo be counterproductive in
VTES, where sideboarding should mean replacing cards of little use at a
particular table with ones useful at a particular table.]

2a. Is there a "cost"?
A cost might be something like using a MPA, paying pool or taking actions.
Taking actions is out - it effectively eliminates the possibility of
sideboarding in stealth, which one would only do if one can't get actions
through without it.
Paying transfers (as an idea) would clearly favor weenie decks, is
therefore unbalanced and can thus be disregarded.
MPAs or paying pool might be options, so might be other things I have
failed to consider.

Personally, I'd favor no cost, or a low cost (see 2c).

2b. How many times a turn can you sideboard?
If there is no cost, or a cost that could be paid multiple times a turn,
this question arises. (I can't think of a cost that is guaranteed to apply
only once a turn.)
At no cost, a "once per turn" limit is necessary (see 2c); personally, I'd
prefer a limit on anthing but a high pool cost.

2c. How many cards can you sideboard per "sideboarding"?
One will not normally want to sideboard on the first 1-3 turns (when it's
not yet apparent what decks one is facing), but will want to be able to
sideboard a good portion of the sideboard befor the endgame - probablz
giving a range of 5-8 turns during which sideboarding would normally take
place.

If sideboarding is free, this'd mean something like 2-3 cards per turn
might be acceptable. if there is a cost, the figure should probably be
higher (making the cost fairly low).

2d. What are the mechanics?
I'd go with removing x cards from the library (either moving them to the
sideboard or removing them from the game... the latter forces more thought
about good sideboarding, because mistakes cannot be rectified), then
adding x cards from the sideboard and shuffling.

As an option, it might be possible to remove some or all cards from
one's hand instead, and redraw after the shuffle (redrawing first makes
little sense... you might draw another copy of the card you're ditching),
which would make sideboarding slightly more powerful.

3. When does sideboarding take place?
During one's own turn, of course, but when exactly?
If there is a MPA cost, the answer is obvious; under all other
circumstances, the question has some significance as to when drawing a
sideboarded card becomes possible.

Before/during the master phase?
Possible redraw before the minion phase, even if sideboarding is from/to
library only.
Before/during the minion phase?
Possible redraw during this phase.
After the minion phase?
Unless removing cards from hand is possible, only one redraw at end of
turn.

---
My suggestion would be:
* 20 card sideboard.
* Sideboard 2 cards once during a turn, with the option to burn 1 pool to
sideboard one additional card. [No cost, with an expensive "upgrade."]
* Sideboarding takes place during the master phase [allows for future sets
to introduce master cards that affect sideboarding, which seems like a
good idea].
* Removing cards from hand is not possible. [Might be abused as a redraw
if opening library draw is bad.]
* Cards sideboarded out go to the sideboard. [Allows sideboarding on early
turns based on "guesses" with the option of getting the cards back into
the deck.]

Thomas

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Thomas wrote:
>>Between-game sideboards will not work, but those are not the only kind.>>

I know in game sideboards are used in certain games--I know Star Trek uses such
a thing, and one of the last, really contriversial promo cards for the B5 CCG
did just that (get a card from outside of the game and put it into play), and
while this too is certainly a possibility, it does one thing better than even
regular (between game) sideboarding does--it makes hoser cards *really*
powerful.

The current batch of VTES hoser cards (Malkavian Dementia, Out of Control,
Letter from Vienna, Ancillae Empowerment, Archon Investigation, whatever) all
are very powerful, but balanced out by their extreme opportunity cost. Whenever
you get to play an Out of Control, it has an incredibly powerful effect, but
the number of times you are going to play it in reality is so limited that
adding it to your deck blind is generally not worth it.

Once you add in a sideboard option, these hoser cards increase in power--their
opportunity cost lessens. You know your opponent is probably going to have a
Malkavian, as you saw their deck before, so putting in a Malkavian Dementia
becomes a good idea, and in all likelyhood, it will be useful.

Now if you go to a plan where you get to put the hoser cards into your deck (or
hand) *during play*, you know *exactly* that these hoser cards will be useful.
You know that your predator is playing with cap <5 !Brujah, as they are already
on the table, so putting that Out of Control into your deck or hand *is* going
to be useful. You know your prey has Lucian in play, so putting that Malk
Dementia in your deck or hand *will* get him killed.

This makes the already quite questionable hoser cards from marginally useful
cards that are very powerful but rarely actually useful into tactical nuclear
strikes, which just isn't a good idea.

The Malkavians simply aren't powerful enough to justify *totally* hosing them
by allowing everyone in the game to strategically add Malkavian Dementias to
their deck during the game when neccessary.

I considered that idea, and while it certainly is a soultion to the problems
caused by scouting and out of game information, it really isn't a particularly
practical (or even possible) plan. Expecting players to submit deck lists ahead
of time, and then get those deck lists out to all the players ahead of time is
asking:

-Everyone to be organized, which we know they aren't.

-Everyone to be willing to do this much work to go to a tournament, which is
unlikely.

-The tournament director to do an awful lot of work before the event, which not
many will be willing to do.

-Everyone to know exactly what deck they will be playing a substantial amount
of time before the event, when we all know that many people, if not all of
them, tweak their decks right up until play starts, even going to an event
hoping to trade for cards to make their deck work at the event.

And how is everyone going to get the decklists before the tournament, let alone
submit their deck lists to the director? E-Mail? Still, not everyone has
reliable access to this. Snail mail? Increases time and costs.

While your idea certainly was a well thought out one, and addresses many of the
flaws of using a sideboard in VTES, it isn't a particularly realistic one.

Messages.Author: Brian
Messages.Body:
Howabout a variant involving a sideboard, instead of a rules change?
I do think the "storyline" tournament was a welcome change (from the
feedback here).

I suggest a sideboard variant something like,

"A player may, up to three times per game, play a card requiring one
or more Disciplines from outside the game."

Make the player choose, say, 10 cards in advance, and not let them
also include those cards in their decks!

If you want to change the "three times per game" and 10 cards, I do
think I set them too conservatively, but remember that setting them
too high would make Tremere Infernal Familiar decks /really/ great.

This variant would let you play Eldritch Glimmer or even Riposte if
circumstances allow, maybe Auspex or Eyes of the Night in a Brujah
deck, actual BLEED in a combat deck without taking up card slots,
Burning Wrath from Emerson Bridges...Ian Forestal would be in
something other than an Ian Forestal deck!

Anything that you wouldn't normally do, either because it's too corner
case (taking up space in your hand) or because you don't have enough
minions that can do it regularly, but you would if you knew you'd ONLY
get the cards when you needed them. It might also make, say,
splashing Bloodlines clans more viable. ("I've only got two Baali in
the crypt, but I can play Daimoinon if I need to").

I'm always a bit annoyed at the idea that my vampire has a given
discipline, but because of who's around, he/she cannot use it.
Homogeny of disciplines doesn't (from a storyline perspective) make a
lot of sense to me.

I'd go so far as to say it's broken, as there's essentially no cost to play it,
and no way to cancel it. The chances of sitting at a table with a deck that
bleeds for 3 or more is reasonable, especially in a tournament. I'm really
surprised more people don't pack at least 3 of these in every deck. The only
reason I don't is that I don't have any (never got much V:TES, and haven't
gotten around to trading for stacks of them just yet).

The others are wallpaper, but they exist as a metagame tool. If Malkavians are
too nasty in your metagame, you pack their hoser, people play them less, you
forget about the hoser and all stays balanced. I usually pack one Malkavian
Dementia in all of my tournament decks. If I played Brujah in a tourney (yeah,
right), I'd probably pack Troile's Revenge as well. Unfortunately, Cultivated
Blood Shortage doesn't make the cut.

In general, you don't get punished for being unlucky, you get punished for
being predictable. People who "randomly" include clan hosers are stupid, but
for the most part those people don't exist. People who pick your clan's hoser
because your clan is overpowered are simply playing the percentages. You
should be less predictable. ;)

If the cards were simply based on luck, they would be extremely annoying, but
their focus is on the metagame, and the general calming effect they are meant
to have if things get out of hand (frex. maybe the designers never expected
Tremere to be an uber-powerful clan with their intercept combat... but just in
case they turned out to be so, Letter From Vienna would tap them all, so they'd
at least need a lot of untap - and it wouldn't hurt the Tremere in general
play, because it'd only get played *if* the Tremere turned out to be too
powerful).

On the other hand, I do like the precedent set forth by Poker (one of the
precedents, that is... I still don't approve of creating specific rules text
for one obscure clan's weakness) of having a decent card with an additional
clan hosing effect on it.

Messages.Body:
Thomas wrote:
>>Presumably, if a card isn't broken now (since AI has never been errated or
banned, presumably, it is not), it shouldn't be broken if sideboards are
introduced.>>

Currently, AI is a card with a very powerful effect--burn a vampire for
effectively zero, if not negative, cost (it works on a vampire bleeding you for
more than 3--it cancels the bleed, saving you pool, and burns the vampire
commiting the action). This very powerful effect is balanced out by its high
opportunity cost. If your predator does not ever bleed you for more than 3,
i.e. they are playing a vote deck, a weenie bleed deck, a responsible S+B deck,
a Rush deck, and Intercept deck, etc, any AIs that you have in your deck and
happen to draw are completely dead cards--you can't even play them just to
cycle them. Thus, including an AI in a deck blindly is a decision of
opportunity cost/effect--is the high opportunity cost (you very well might not
be able to play it) outweighed by the effect or neccessity of the card? Often,
the answer is no.

Now once you include sideboarding, the opportunity cost of the card becomes
*much* less severe--you can leave AIs in your sideboard until you *know* that
you are sitting next to a deck that is very likely to bleed you for more than 3
per action. You then slap some AIs in your deck, and you suddenly have a very
powerful effect (save pool and burn vampires) with a nullified opportunity cost
(as you know what deck you are sitting next to, and you know the AIs are going
to be playable).

Thus, by changing the environment the card is in (i.e. adding sideboarding
rules) you reduce the opportunity cost and increase the utility and power of
the card.

The seven clan hosers in Jyhad were:

Ventrue - Cultivated Blood Shortage
Malkavian - Malkavian Dementia
Brujah - Brujah Frenzy
Tremere - Letter from Vienna
Toreador - Tragic Love Affair
Nosferatu - Nosferatu Putrescence
Gangrel - Gangrel Devolution

...and there may be some more that I don't remember. Overall, they were
basically balanced from design intent, although Malkavian Dementia ends
up having a significantly larger effect than all the others.

In an "Original" environment, Gangrel Devolution would have been much
more significant, as Gangrel inherently had little way to increase their
bleed. Letter from Vienna would have made short work of Tremere
intercept/combat decks. Tragic Love Affair is a "don't untap" card, and
with no stealth available to the Toreador, it would have been difficult
to gain the Edge against a Methuselah who was willing to defend. Brujah
Frenzy would be very irritating when trying to oust someone and very
beneficial to the card-player, especially if you were forced to enter
combat with your own predator. The Ventrue card seems to be direct bait
for the three interceptor clans, although the design team clearly didn't
foresee the heavy use of Voter Captivation and 5th Tradition that goes
on in the average Ventrue deck. But that's been a given for awhile,
that the design team didn't expect the HUGE piles of cards that people
were willing to collect for the game. Nosferatu Putrescence probably
has the least effect of any, but it is also the sole non-Master card and
the most easily cyclable in multiples if necessary.

to include at least one clan hoser (preferably chosen to impact the clan

You're right. That is the dispute. To me, this is an insufficient definition.
A card can oust all of your opponents and retroactively take away victory points
previously won by them and give you an immediate sweep of the table and I would
call that a highly powerful effect. But if, on the other hand, it is so difficult
to play as to make unlikely anyone will ever accomplish it (say, flip 30 coins and
have them all come up heads: a one in a billion shot), then it can not be called
balance. Balance is balance, equality between difficulty in using and the
magnitude of the effect. Just show the effect is powerful, no matter how powerful,
is insufficient to prove balance and incorrect to call balance when the difficulty
of using it effectively is even more extreme.

opposing vampire for a turn is insufficient in comparison to the difficulty

reference to how important is it to do so given the costs involved in replaying
games. I don't consider it important enough to justify replaying games.

>> And, one other thing. Everyone makes the finals. So, the only benefit to
>> playing the prelim games is to determine who gets to choose seating.
>Except,
>> whoever does well in the prelims will likely be considered the greatest
>threat,
>> which should remove any advantage in getting to choose seating.
>
>Well, as you say, table management probably becomes a big
>thing, but that would be the case regardless of how you
>determined the finals and how much you did beforehand.
>You're right, though, that it's probably not going to be
>that much of an advantage to be able to pick your seating
>for this kind of final game, and as such, you might as
>well cut to the chase pretty quickly in terms of how many
>games you're going to play before "the one that counts".
>
>I do think it'd be worthwhile to at least have *one* game
>before the final, though, so that all the interesting effects
>get a chance to come into play in the final, ie so that it's
>*not* just a neutral-starting-point game. (IOW I would have
>no problem with the introduction of a 1-preliminary-round
>option for VEKN tournaments, whether or not they felt the
>need to limit its use to small tournaments.)

I don't see it as interesting. The games will just see the same card
interactions over and over. The only thing that might be interesting is seeing
how well players execute their adjusted strategies given full knowledge of what
everyone else's decks are designed to do. In other words, see if who you
predict to win actually wins. This, to me, is of interest to an observer but
not necessarily of any interest to the players. Something for computers to do
- run a simulation of what would happen when these 4-5 decks are played against
each other in every possible seating position.

news:20020403144745...@mb-mc.aol.com...

> To an extent. I enjoy CCGs a lot more when I don't know what's going to
> happen. Given full knowledge of the decks, the personality of the players
> involved, and where they are seated, I have a pretty good idea of what is
> likely to happen.

In most of the games my regular group plays, most people are
playing decks they've played several times before. (since
hardly any of us have time to make lots of new decks each
week.) This means that we often have all of the knowledge
mentioned above, but I still find the games interesting...
there's a lot going on in the actual playing that interests
me, and a substantial-enough amount of variability just in
how the decks come up/interact on different occasions. (I
should probably qualify this by saying that most people
also have enough different (if recurring) decks that we
don't often "repeat a game" on a given night in the sense
of the same people with the same decks on the same table,
but "repeat games" in different weeks are certainly not
inconceivable.)

Now, I'd certainly also say that games can be more
unpredictable, and therefore potentially (though not really
necessarily) more interesting, when no one is already
familiar with what anyone else is playing. But that's not
even achievable for us, most of the time, and it's not,
for me, the only thing that makes a game of VTES fun or
interesting.

> >Or is it more an issue of playing against the same people
> >each time that causes this behavior, rather than that they're
> >playing the same decks each time?
>
> I'd rather play against the same people with different decks than the same
> decks with different people, though I don't think that's what you are
getting
> at.

No, it wasn't exactly; I was just trying to get a handle on
whether what you found boring or table-management-causing
or whatever was objectionable was caused mainly just by the
one-table-tournament games being played by the same *people*
every time, or if it relied on them also playing the same
*decks* every time. Which I think is answered by what you
said, anyway.

> My take on everyone playing the same decks is that you are conducting an
> exercise rather than playing a game. Theoretically interesting, it's a
bore to
> play as players know too much and adopt strategies based on their excess
> knowledge. Also, while you learn something from such an exercise, what
you
> don't learn is how the tournament would have turned out if the players
didn't
> have full knowledge of each others' decks.

No, naturally. I don't always find it a bore to play, since
to me (as I just wrote a moment ago) a lot of the game's
interest is in the actual play, not just in how deck X
interacts with deck Y in theory or on average. Which obviously
doesn't invalidate your feeling that it *is* boring, I just
apparently don't find it as boring as you do. :-)

> I don't see it as interesting. The games will just see the same card
> interactions over and over. The only thing that might be interesting is
seeing
> how well players execute their adjusted strategies given full knowledge of
what
> everyone else's decks are designed to do. In other words, see if who you
> predict to win actually wins. This, to me, is of interest to an observer
but
> not necessarily of any interest to the players. Something for computers
to do
> - run a simulation of what would happen when these 4-5 decks are played
against
> each other in every possible seating position.

Well, this is all true if what you're interested in is only
the abstract "who/what deck should win" and then what/who
wins "on average". It's less true if you see the gameplay
as an end (or at least topic) in itself. To me, there are
in most games of VTES a lot of decisions that are *not*
simply matters of correct vs incorrect, even when you know
what your opponents' decks "are about"; no one's deck is
so predictable as to always have exactly what it "should"
have and so information is always somewhat limited; beyond
that, even given perfect information, reasonable players can
have different opinions on the best course of action to
take in any given situation. There's always the possibility
of simple mistakes, misjudgments, and immediately-regretted
foolishness, but those aren't the only things (IMO) that can
determine the course of games like these.

For whatever that's worth.
